case_source: (On appeal from the judgment and order dated 4-12-74 of the High Court Division passed in Petition No. 6 of 1974).
full_judgment:
Mahmud Husain, C. J.—This appeal by special leave is against a judgment of the Constitution Bench of the High Court Division. The respondent was first appointed on a temporary basis as a Deputy Director under the appellant which was then called 'East Pakistan Small Industries Corporation and he was confirmed after 2 years of service and attached to the Yarn Distribution Cell and on 14-9-72 he was entrusted with certain duties, namely, (1) Supervision of the work of the Field Inspector for verification of applications of weavers; (2) Supervision in respect of distribution of ration cards by the Y. D. Cs. and checking up of the statements and returns thereto and to apprise J. D. Y (P&A) of the weekly progress; (3) Attending to public complaints and investigation of the same as and when necessary with the approval of J. D. Y (P & A); (4) Inspection of Y. D. Cs. on specific assignments and (5) Any other work that may be assigned to him by J. D. Y (P&A) from time to time (Nazmul Hussain) J. D. Y (P&A). The distribution centers were placed under Yarn Distribution Committees which were put under the control of local respectable persons. Mr. Safar Ali, the then Member of the Constituent Assembly was placed in-charge of Narsingdi Yarn Distribution Committee as Chairman who requested the respondent to recommend the eases of genuine weavers for allotment of yarn. The respondent was placed under suspension with immediate effect on charges of misconduct and corruption by a memo dated 4-11-72 and was informed that formal proceedings were being drawn up against him. The charges were formally communicated by a memo dated 13-11-72. It was alleged that the petitioner had allotted a few bales of yarn to different persons in weaving factories and thus misused his official position which amounted to misconduct and corruption as well as inefficiency and was asked to show cause as to why he should not be removed from the service of the appellant or otherwise be suitably punished under rule 25 of the Bangladesh Small Industries Services Regulations, 1965. On 22-11-72 the respondent submitted written explanation denying the charges level-led against him. He submitted that he did not pass any order of allotment himself but he merely recommended certain applications which was not done with any dishonest intention. Thereafter the respondent was directed to appear before the Inquiry Officer appointed by the Corporation and the respondent accordingly appeared before the Enquiry Officer who recorded his statement and examined applications containing his recommendations thereon for allotment of few bales of yarn to different weavers or factories. The Enquiry Officer did not examine any of the applicants whose cases the appellant had recommended nor did he examine any member of the Allotment Committee. The Enquiry Officer by his report dated 24-1-73 gave the following findings on each of the following cases referred to him:-

"(i) Case of Mr. Sattar Weaving Factory :-The noting ('2 bales may be allotted') of Mr. Choudhury, does not appear to be regular, since he is not authorised to take any action on the letter of the party addressed Narsingdi Centre, thus Mr. Choudhury has not maintained office decorum. (ii) Case of Mr. Ali Akbar :-This instruction (Mr. Awal will kindly allot 3 bales) appears to be an order to a Junior Officer for allotment for which Mr. Choudhury is not competent to issue such instruction, his action was uncalled for.

(iii) Case of M/s. Fatema Weaving Factory:- “An application for allotment on which Mr. Choudhury notes as follows :-`May be allowed'  The action of Mr. Choudhury appears to be irregular.

(iv) M/s. Ahmed and M/s. Sujan Weaving Factory:-`After examinations of these two cases it is found that Mr. Choudhury recommended both the cases as follows—`one bale may be considered' this recommendation cannot be termed as an order for allotment. That no opinion was ex-pressed on the 5th count of the charges, that there might be similar other cases of your orders for allotment"

And thereafter in conclusion he stated as follows:-

"Mr. Choudhury by taking actions in the parties' applications violated the office decorum and discipline. In case of Mr. Ali Akbar, Mr. Choudhury was not competent enough to issue direct instruction by passing 5. D. Y. (P&A). In other cases his noting in the applications appear to be uncalled for. In none of the above cases any evidence of corruption could be established."

2. The second show cause notice was served upon the respondent on 13-3-73 proposing a penalty of dismissal. On 13-4-73, the respondent received a notice from the First Screening Board of the Government of Bangladesh charging him under Articles 5(A) and 5(I) of the Government of Bangladesh (Services Screening) Order, 1972, President's Order No. 67 of 1972. The respondent appearing before the Screening Board on 8-5-73 denied the charges of corruption and misconduct. Thereafter the respondent received an order of dismissal dated 31-5-73 from service of the Corporation with immediate effect.

3. It appears that the order of dismissal was passed pursuant to the decision of Board of Directors and in consideration of the recommendations of the First Screening Board constituted by the Government. The learned Judges of the High Court Division on consideration of the affidavits declared the impugned order dated 11-5-1973 dismissing the respondent from the service of the Corporation to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

<u>4. The appellant-corporation moved this Division for special leave to appeal and accordingly leave was granted to consider as to whether the respondent being an employee of a Statutory Corporation, the relation between him and the Corporation was one of Master and Servant, and whether the High Court Division had jurisdiction to interfere with the order of dismissal under Article 102 of the Constitution. The learned Attorney-General did not press the second point as to the maintainability of the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution in view of the fact that the statutory Corporation has now by amendment of the General Clauses Act is regarded a Local Authority.</u>

5. This appeal has been heard along with Civil Appeal No. 7 of 1975, which has arisen out of a suit instituted by a dismissed employee against The Managing Director, Janata Bank and involves the consideration of almost the same question of law. The arguments advanced in the latter appeal also are being considered in this judgment, although the said appeal is being disposed of by a separate order.

6. To appreciate the sole point for consideration, now that Mr. Attorney-General has conceded the question of maintainability of the Writ Petition under Article 102, we are to gather the principles from the leading judicial authorities in the matter as there is no direct law on the subject. No doubt, some help could be obtained from section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. A legal character could be claimed and declaration obtained from Court under this section. It cannot be disputed that where a writ lies for a declaration of nullity, a suit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act equally lies. The point is when and under what circumstances can an employee of a statutory Corporation maintain an action for a declaration of nullity. The principles can be gathered on a reference to English decisions as embodied in leading cases. Decisions of Indian and Pakistan Courts may also be of assistance. On this question learned Counsel of both sides have cited a number of decisions and referred to some leading text books. We are first to refer to those authorities and then try to formulate the principles with reference to the laws of our country.

<u>7. Mr. Attorney-General has referred to a text book entitled Government Enterprise, Comparative Study, edited by W. Friedmann and J. F. Garner and has cited the passage:</u>

The most likely field for State enterprise in an expanding economy is where private enterprise is undeveloped : in new industries and new products where the risks are great and the private entrepreneur—in an age of capital scarcity and high taxation of profits —may well hang back. This is no doubt one of the major motives for establishing a public corporation, and other forms of Government enterprise. The variety of forms in which the various States have, at different times, proceeded to establish public enterprises is almost infinite, but three main types emerge to which almost every public enterprise approximates: (1) departmental administration ; (2) the joint stock company controlled completely or partly by public authority; and finally (3) the public corporation proper, as a distinct type of corporation different from the private law company It appears to be a, universal practice that public corporations are created either by special statute or by a Government Ordinance. Unlike the commercial company they do not automatically come into existence by fulfilling certain statutory requirements. The creation of a public undertaking by special statute serves to distinguish the public corporation proper from the public undertaking which is established under the company law though the State provides the entire capital and holds all or virtually all the shares directly or through one of its own undertakings. The public corporations in the common law jurisdictions have entirely followed the rule that their employees should not have the status of civil servants. This is an outcome of the conception that the corporations should, as far as possible, approximate to the ideas of business management and not to be tied too closely to the civil service. But, there seems no present intention of changing this status. Nevertheless, service in the public corporations is not the same as service in a commercial company. It is a form of public service."

<u>8. Mr. Attorney-General has also referred to another text book by M. P. Jain and S. N. Jain, Principles of Administrative Law, (Second Edition), which dealt with the subject with special reference to Indian conditions. The passage cited by him is:</u>

"The main disadvantages in departmentally run enterprises are rigidity of procedures, red tape and delay in taking and implementing decisions. All this arises because government procedures are applied to departmental enterprises and the proverbial red tape comes into vogue even in such cases which may not be conducive to the efficient management of a commercial enterprise. The staff of a departmental enterprise consists of civil servants whose terms of recruitment and conditions of service are the same as those of the other government servants. It is thus not possible to promote any one on merit or take prompt disciplinary action against any one when necessary. All these rigid procedures do not accord with accepted commercial or trading norms. These hamper individual judgment and initiative and taking of quick decisions which are necessary for the successful operation of a business enterprises. Thus departmental form of running commercial enterprise is, therefore, regarded as unsuitable. It has become necessary to use the technique of establishing autonomous bodies to run a business on behalf of the Government so as to give it commercial freedom. The system has grown because of the need to ensure freedom and flexibility of approach for an undertaking so that it may act with necessary expedition and initiative. A government company has most of the features of a private limited company and can function with the same initiative and freedom. Its employees are not civil servants. It can have its own rules of recruitment, promotion and dismissal of its employees. It is generally exempt from the budget accounting and audit procedures applicable to government departments. These advantages are ensured in case of a public corporation as well. The usual pattern of managing the affairs of a public undertaking is to have an apex body, a governing board, for the purpose. In case of government companies such boards are known as boards of directors and resemble similar boards in other private companies The position is now well established that the entity of government companies and statutory corporations is distinct and separate from the government and, therefore, the employees of a public undertaking are not regarded as civil servants and the protection of article 311 of the Constitution does not extend to them. (Vide Mafatlal Vs. Divisional Controller State Transport Corporation in A.I.R. 1966 S C. 1964). It has also been held that section 50 of the D. V. C. Act, 1948 which provides that the employees of the Corporation "shall be deemed., when acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the 'Act, to Fe-public servants within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code" would not bring the servants of a statutory corporation concerned within the fold of Article 311 of the Constitution of India. In that context we are also of the view that section 41(A) of the Act having similar provision as in section 50 of the D. V. C. Act cannot bring the respondent within the meaning of public servant. It has been held in the case of Rajasthan State Electricity Board, Jaipur Vs. Mohan Lal and others reported in A. I. R. 1967 S.C. 1857 that the Board as a statutory body comes within the purview of other authority under Article 12 of the Constitution of India and as such, such right can be enforced against it by a person affected."

9. Mr. Khondker has referred to Halsbury's Laws of England and, it may be noted, Halsbury's Laws of England Third Edition Volume 25 paragraph 929 provides in this behalf :-

"Except where it is otherwise provided by statute, officers in the employment of the Crown hold their offices at the pleasure of the Crown, and are in general subject to dismissal at any time without cause assigned. Officers of local authorities usually hold their office during pleasure of the local authority. Employees of national corporations are not in the position of civil servants and do not hold office at the pleasure of the Crown; but if the posts of such employees are offered to them as permanent pensionable posts on conditions which included powers of dismissal for specified reasons, the power of dismissal on reasonable notice, which is incident to a general hiring otherwise than for a year, may be excluded on the construction of the contract of appointment."

Further reference to Halsbury's Laws of England Third Edition Volume 9 paragraph 6 which refers to National Corporations may be made:

"National Corporations.

In recent years a new class of corporations, has come into prominence. Corporations of this class are corporations aggregate, are created by Act of Parliament or by charter for the benefit or service of the community and are not, or are not now, owned by private individuals. Those corporations are here described as national corporations so as to limit the class to those corporations whose activities are not less than nation wise, but so as to include corporations which are part of a group having such activities, and so as to exclude, for example, development corporations for new towns whose purposes are local but which in many respects are similar corporations. "National corporations are public service corporations and carry on their undertakings as responsible independent corporations, not as part of any department of State. They may, however, be concerned with the execution of policy of the Government within the field of their activities, as for example, in the case of monetary policy, is the Bank of England, but in matters of routine, in the ordinary running of their undertakings and in the decisions necessary for that purpose, they act independently of the Government. They are usually subject, nevertheless, in some measure to the control of a department of State for which a Minister or other member of the Cabinet is responsible to Parliament, who commonly appoints the members of the national corporations and has the power to give it directions."

<u>10. Exigencies of modern Welfare State, which aims at harmonising democratic process with socialist economy have forced the State to undertake various economic, social and public health measures on national scale. Sometimes existing undertakings are nationalised to achieve the welfare goal. The preamble and fundamental principles of state policy of the corporation, directive in nature, intend to achieve a socialist economic system within the rule of law. Many countries of the world notably England, Sweden and India in varying degrees of accentuation and using different terminology have intended to achieve the welfare goal. Experiments in these countries and study of their legislative attempts will be of great assistance for our courts to formulate principles of interpretation of legislation aiming to achieve a socialist economy within the Rule of Law.</u>

<u>11. Study of techniques adopted by the Government indicates that one of the methods applied is to set up corporations. Broadly speaking they are called public corporations in contradistinction with private corporations set up under Companies Act by the citizens. The State policy is to utilise the principle of corporation. A corporation has its own independent existence distinct from the share holders or directors or administrators and has all the attributes of a juristic personality. A statutory corporation therefore is neither a dependent on Government nor its Agent unless there is something expressly contrary in the statute vide Tamlin Vs. Hannaford 1950(i) K. B. 18.</u>

<u>12. Public Corporations set up by the State again may assume various forms. It may choose to set up a corporation under the Companies Act either contributing entire share capital by the Government or dividing the contribution of share capital between the Government and the public. It may set up a Corporation by a statute This statutory corporation again is sometimes made amenable to different provisions of the Companies Act subject to the statute and sometimes it is kept totally outside the ambit of operation of the Companies Act, governable wholly by the incorporating statute itself. A public corporation may function as a Government department or its agent or both or may be totally independent of either having its own independent corporate personality.</u>

<u>13. We therefore find that a public corporation is a hybrid organism showing some of the features of a Government Department and some of a business company and standing outside the ordinary framework of Central and Local Government. As an administrative device it has been used for very long years but it has in particular come into prominence after independence from the British rules and also liberation of Bangladesh. Its purpose is to enable some industries or social service body to run for the benefit of the public but without the constraint of the parliamentary investigation and criticism to which it would be subject to if it were merely a Government Department, like the Post Office. In the case of an industry it must be master in its own house and there must be enough independence to encourage bold and farsighted decisions, subject only to the public interest. Thus there is a distinction between broad policy and day-to-day administration, the former being the sphere of the Government (and therefore the parliament) and the latter being the sphere of independent self management. In the case of social service, there must be devolution of responsibility so that there may be sonic degree of local independence with the necessary central control. The principle of corporation offers scope for many kinds of governmental experiment under which central control, local control and total independence can be blended in desired proportions.</u>

<u>14. Paragraph 871 Halsbury's Laws of England Volume 25 Third Edition also says that a person may be a servant to different masters and a contract for exclusive personal service does not necessarily establish the relation of master and servant. Paragraph 872 of the said Volume provides that the relationship of master and servant is characterised by a contract of service, express or implied, between the master and servant. A contract of service is one in which a person under-takes to serve another and to obey his reasonable orders within the scope of the duty under-taken. Whether Or not a particular contract is a contract of service is a question of fact, depending upon the terms of the engagement, the method of remuneration, and the power of controlling and dismissing the worker, although none of these factors is by itself conclusive.</u>

15. Before dealing with the arguments of Mr. Attorney-General on the question of applicability of the master and servant rule to the employee of a Statutory Corporation, let us first dispose of the point urged at the bar as to whether such employees are entitled to the constitutional guarantee, as incorporated in Article 135 of the Constitution. it has been strenuously urged that various Presidential Orders and enactments such as President's Order No. 9 of 1972, President's Order No. 14 of 1972, President's Order No. 67 of 1972, President's Order No. 93 of 1972, Act 12 of 1974 and Act 38 of 1974, have clothed such employees with the status of 'Government Servants or 'Public Servants' and that such a status perforce entitles them to the benefit of the said constitutional guarantee. It should however be observed that the status of a Public Servant or a Government Servant has not been conferred generally upon an employee of a Statutory Corporation by the said Acts or Presidential Orders but have been so done for the purposes of the particular enactments. It has been made clear in the definition clause itself in each of these enactments, by prefacing the definition clause with the words, "In this Order" or "In this Act", as the case may be. Such definitions cannot therefore be read into the provisions of the Constitution and the status of a Government or Public Servant be attributed to the employees of a Statutory Corporation for the purpose of the constitutional provision of Article 135. This is also in accord with the well recognised rule of construction of a statute.

<u>16. It would, however, be noticed that there is no reference to 'Government Servant' or 'Public Servant' in Article 135. It is a person. holding a civil post in the service of the Republic who is entitled to the protection provided in the said Article, and 'the service of the Republic has been defined in Article 152 of the Constitution as "any service, post or office, whether in a civil or military capacity, in respect of the Government of Bangladesh, and any other service declared by law to be a service of the Republic'. Article 135 contemplates, therefore, such service, post or office as is concerned with the governance or administration of Bangladesh as a State, and employees of Statutory Corporations which are set up by a modern State to carry out certain objects outside its traditional administrative responsibility can hardly come within the scope of the said definition. It is to be noted that the Acts or President's Orders to which reference has been made have scrupulously avoided any declaration of the service under a Statutory Corporation as a service of the Republic.</u>

17. The subject relating to the relationship between a public statutory corporation and its employees does not appear to present a uniform picture as to the nature of the relief such employees can claim in a court of law in case of their exclusion from service and the judicial views on this question, particularly in England, India and Pakistan, which we have had the opportunity to examine in the instant case to some extent, even though not exhaustively, indicate a tendency of swaying from one side to the other, from time to time.

<u>18. The American Courts do not appear to make any distinction between the public or private character of the corporation for the purpose of granting the relief of reinstatement of a dismissed employee or other reliefs particularly under the writ jurisdiction of the superior courts, whereas the English Courts have generally maintained a distinction in this regard. Following passage from the Law of Extra-ordinary Legal Remedies (1926) by Ferris referring to the law relating to the writ of Mandamus as practised in the state Courts of the United States will bear this out:</u>

<u>"Mandamus is the proper remedy to prevent further illegal exclusion from office in a private corporation when the right thereto is clear, although under such circumstances there may be an incumbent. The same principles as applicable to public offices in such cases are applicable here (at page 328).</u>

<u>The following passage relating to the writ of quo warranto may also be usefully quoted from the same book :</u>

<u>"The English rule is, that to justify quo warranto to try title to an office; it is essential that the office be such as the law deems of a public nature, and quo warranto will not lie, although the charter is derived from the sovereign if the sovereign neither aids nor reserves any control over it.</u>

<u>All American courts, with one exception, Massachusetts, agree that an action of quo warranto, or in the nature thereof, is the proper remedy to test the right of office in a private corporation, on the theory that any corporation chartered or organised under the laws of a state is public in character, and any abuse or usurpation thereof is an abuse or usurpation of the State's privilege."</u>

19. According to the English practice, however, the nature of the public character of a corporation is not determined by the nature of its origin and the policy of the law, but by the nature or purpose of its business. When a corporation is invested with some portion of the sovereign functions of the Government which is to be exercised by the corporation for the benefit of the public such a corporation may be said to have a public character, but a corporation, which, though instituted under a law of the country, is a body of certain individuals organised for the purpose of private benefits cannot be said to possess a public character. In a public corporation, very often the ultimate control is in the hands of the Government.

20. The English law in this regard has been stated in the Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd Edition Volume 11 in paragraph 162 in the following words:

"An order of mandamus will lie to compel the restoration of a person to an office or franchise, whether spiritual or temporal, of which he has been wrongfully dismissed, provided the office or franchise is of public nature, as for example to the office of mayor, alderman, recorder, town clerk, burgess or other municipal position, to academical degree, to a fellowship of college where there is no visitor, or the offices of parish clerk and sexton."

<u>21. The law of master and servant, as applicable for determining the right of an employee dismissed from service is based upon the view that such a right is exclusively founded upon a contract of service between an employer and an employee and that inasmuch as such a contract is incapable of being specifically enforced under the provision of the Specific Relief Act, an action for restoration of the dismissed employee to its former office is not maintainable in law. It conceives a private individual serving another private individual or body for mutual private benefits and the relationship does not involve any element other than the contractual one. In such a case, the employee is interested only in his remuneration, which can be measured solely in monetary value. In the same way, the employer employs the particular individual for his own private purpose which is exclusively his own concern and in which nobody else is interested, and if, in case of a breach of any contractual obligation arising out of the contract of employment, the employer is prepared to forego the service of his employee and at the same time pay the dismissed employee adequate monetary compensation, it is nobody else's business to be concerned about it. But if the office of employment has got a public character, the relationship transcends the confines of a contractual character and ceases to be the concern of the individuals, namely, the person who dismisses and the person who is dismissed. In such a case, the person who exercises the power of dismissal does so on behalf of a public corporation in which the general public or a substantial section of the general public is interested and such power is exercised under some authority of law. He cannot rest cynically content by saying that it is the personal affair of an individual or some individuals whose representative he is, and he is prepared to pay the dismissed employee the necessary compensation, if the order of dismissal is ultimately found to be illegal and that it is nobody else's business to be bothered about it. The position of the employee is also different from that of one serving a private concern, at least in principle, as he is serving an institution of public benefit in the development and progress of which he also is supposed to be, interested. Those are the considerations which naturally lift the cases of public employment out of the strict category of the master and servant rule. In such a case, the terms and conditions of service may also be regulated by some statutory provisions, and the termination of service may be made in violation of such provisions. In that event as well the master and servant rule cannot be invoked in order to deny the relief of reinstatement to the discharged employee. It may be also that the office itself has been created by the Statute where the employee will undoubtedly have a kind of legal status the rights whereof may be capable of being enforced.</u>

<u>22. It may however so happen that in spite of the office being a statutory one or of public character, the terms and conditions of the office or some of them may be regulated by contract and not by way of statutory provisions, in which case the violation of any of the said terms, including the termination of the office, should be looked upon as nothing more than a mere breach of the contract and an action for specific performance of the said contract by reinstating the employee in his former office is not available to him.</u>

<u>23. The case of dismissal from the office of a statutory corporation of a public character by giving a charge, however, stands on a different footing and an action for reinstatement may be competent, notwithstanding the fact that the terms and conditions of the said office are regulated by a contract, because the principle of natural justice, audi altarem partem is attracted in such a case he substance of this principle is expressed in the maxim no one shall be condemned unheard and it means that when a person or a body of persons is invested by some statutory provision with a power to make an order or take a decision which may affect the right or property of another person adversely the exercise of such power is coupled with a duty of acting judicially and of following the principle of natural justice in making the said order or taking the said decision. Simple termination of service without giving a blame or stigma, even though illegal or irregular, will not attract the operation of the principle of natural justice in such a case.</u>

<u>24. These principles as have been referred to above, have been by and large, incorporated in the law of judicial review as contained in Article 102(2) of the Constitution. This constitution power of a superior court can be invoked and the necessary direction or declaration can be given or made only against a person performing functions in connection with the affair of the Republic or of a local authority. The public character of the functionary against whom the necessary relief can be given under the constitutional power is manifest from the terms of the constitutional provision itself, as it requires that such functionary must be acting in the discharge of some public duties relating to the affairs of the State. The term local authority has not been defined in the Constitution but according to the definition as given in section 3(31) of the General Clauses Act it is clear that such term implies a public duty authorised by law or by the Government to carry on some administrative functions. A public corporation, as we have already noticed, is entrusted with some portion of the sovereign function of the Government which is to be performed by the Corporation for the benefit of the public and such a corporation is undoubtedly a person performing functions in relation to the affairs of the Republic within the meaning of Article 102(2) of the Constitution. What-ever uncertainty there might have been in regard to such an interpretation has now been removed by an amendment of the definition clause to the effect that a local authority includes a statutory body. Once it is accepted that an appropriate order under Article 102(2) of the Constitution may be made against a public corporation the court may make an order restraining it from doing what is not permitted by law to do or directing it to do what it is required by law to do or declaring that an act done or a proceeding taken by a public corporation has been done or taken without any lawful authority. Dismissal of an employee of such a corporation in violation of statutory rules or regulations is actionable for the purpose of restoration to office according to the constitutional mandate. Dismissal of an employee in violation of the principle of natural justice is also actionable in a similar way as the principle of natural justice must be regarded as a part of the statute, unless it is excluded therefrom by specific words.</u>

25. We may now turn to some of the leading decisions on the question of English, Indian and Pakistani jurisdiction, and, to begin with, we may consider some of the more important decisions of the English Courts. We may first of all refer to the celebrated case decided by House of Lords in Vine Vs. National Dock Labour Board, 1957 A.C. 188. Plaintiff, Vine, a dock labourer employed in the reserve pool by the defendants, the National Dock Labour Board, under the scheme set up by the Dock Workers (Regulation of Employment) Order, 1947, was allocated work with a stevedoring company , but defaulting to report to them, a complaint was lodged with the defendants, and was heard by a disciplinary committee appointed by the local Dock Labour Board, who upheld the complaint and, purporting to act under clause 16(2)(c) of the Order gave the plaintiff Vine notice to terminate his employment with the defendants. His appeal to a tribunal set up under the scheme was dismissed. He started proceedings against the defendant claiming damages for wrongful dismissal and a declaration that his reported dismissal was illegal, ultravires and void. The trial Judge awarded him damages and granted a declaration. The Court of Appeal held that damages were a sufficient remedy and that a declaration should not be granted. Reversing the decision of the Court of Appeal, the House of Lords held, that the plaintiff's dismissal was invalid, since the local Dock Labour Board had no power under the scheme, to delegate to a disciplinary committee their disciplinary powers given by clause 16 of the Order, under which a man might be entirely excluded from the employment of a dock worker. It was further held, that although it might be that the discretion to give a declaratory judgment should be exercised sparingly, in the present case having regard to the background of the scheme, it was found pro-per that in addition to awarding damages the court should declare the plaintiff's rights. In this case of Vine Vs. National Dock Labour Board 1957 A.C. 488, the application of the master and servant rule was excluded because of the statutory intervention.

26. Viscount Kilimuir L.J. explained the law in his speech before the House in the following words at pp. 500-501 of the report:

"First it follows from the fact that the plaintiff's dismissal was invalid, that his name was never validly removed and that he continued in the employ of the National Board. This is an entirely different situation from the ordinary master and servant case; there if the master wrongfully dismissed the servant either summarily or by giving insufficient notice, the employment is effectually terminated, albeit in breach of contract. Here the removal of the plaintiff's name from the register being in law a nullity he continued to have the right to be treated as registered dock worker with all the benefits which by statute, that status conferred in him. It is therefore right that with the background of this scheme the court should declare his rights.

Secondly, it was said that the declaration would lead to further litigation; I cannot believe that the National Board would do other than comply with the declaration and in that case, I do not see why there should be further litigation.

Thirdly, for the reasons given by Jenkins L.J. I found it difficult to see that damages would be an adequate remedy. Lord Keith of Avonholm made the following observation in his speech in this case at pp 507-508 of the report:

"This is not a straightforward relationship of master and servant. Normally, and apart from the intervention of a statute, there would never be a nullity in terminating an ordinary contract of master and servant. Dismissal might be in breach of a contract and so unlawful but would only found in damages. Here we are concerned with a statutory scheme of employment."

<u>27. It is clear from this case that the statutory provisions regulating the service conditions of an employee exclude the operation of the ordinary master and servant rule. It has been mentioned on behalf of the appellants that the principle of Vine's case is not attracted in the instant case, in view of the fact that the relationship between the National Dock Labour Board and the plaintiff was not strictly that of a master and his servant and that the Board was merely a registering authority with whom all the Dock labourers were to register themselves in anticipation of future employment. This contention of the learned Counsel for the appellants has got no force whatsoever. A mere glance at the various provisions of the Order under which the scheme was set up reveals that a dock labourer is employed in the reserve pool by the National Dock Labour Board and he is registered with the Board for the purpose that he is available for work. He receives payment from the Board for unemployment or under employment and is required to carry out the directions of the Local Board, in default whereof the Local Board may withhold payment or suspend him without pay or terminate his employment after giving 7 days notice or dismiss him summarily. There is hardly any scope for doubt that the relationship between a registered dock labourer and the National Dock Labour Board, despite certain formal differences from that between an ordinary employer and employee, is essentially that of an employer and employee. The said case is undoubtedly an authority for the proposition that the breach of the service condition of an employee, which has got a statutory cover excludes the operation of the ordinary master and servant rule.</u>

28. The next important English case which has been cited before us is Barbar Vs. Manchester Regional Hospital Board and another 1958 1 All. E.R. 322 decided by the Queen's Bench Division. Barbar was employed as a consultant at a hospital administered by a local authority subject to the terms and conditions stated in a Memorandum issued by the Minister and it was held in the said case that the breach of clause 16 of the terms contained in the said Memorandum was nothing more than a breach of a contract between a master and a servant. The facts were that consequent on the establishment of the National Health Service on July 5, 1948, Manchester Regional Hospital Board, a regional hospital board, offered by a circular letter dated July 1, 1949 to continue the appointment among other persons of the plain-tiff, Barber who at the time was employed as a consultant at a hospital administered by a local authority, which, thereafter, came under the administration of the Board on behalf of Minister of Health. The continuance of Barber's employment was subject to the terms and conditions of the service of medical staff stated in a Memorandum of June, 1949, issued by the Minister. By clause 16 of those terms, the consultant, who considered that his appointment was being unfairly terminated by a Regional Hospital Board, was entitled to send a full statement of the facts to the Minister, who was then to place the case before a professional committee for their advice, in the light of which he would decide whether to confirm the termination of service, or to direct reinstatement, or to arrange some third solution agreeable to the parties concerned. This proceeding was to be completed before a Board's decision to terminate a consultant's service was carried into effect. The plaintiff Barber continued in the employment of the Board as Hospital consultant. In January 1952, the Board purported to terminate the plaintiff's employment as from April 30, 1952 and the plaintiff considering his dismissal unfair, caused, the Minister to be informed of the facts, but it was maintained on behalf of the Minister that no appeal lay to him, and the Minister, therefore, reached no decision under clause 16. The plaintiff brought an action against the Board and the Minister, claiming declaration that his employment with the Board was subject to the terms and conditions of service issued by the Minister and that it was never validly deter-mined. He also claimed damages for breach of contract for wrongful dismissal and, as against the Minister, a declaration that in failing to comply with clause 16, the Minister acted in breach of his statutory duty under the National Health Service Act, 1964. Distinguishing the case of Vine Vs. National Dock Labour Board (1956) 3 All. E.R. 939, it was held by the Queen's Bench Judge that the contract of Barber with the Board was one between Master and Servant, the termination of which could not be a nullity, and the plaintiff was not, therefore, entitled to a declaration that his employment had never been validly determined, but was entitled only to recover damages for breah of contract. The case of Vine Vs. National Dock Labur Board was distinguished in this case in the following manner:

"Giving the matter the best consideration that I can I am unable to equate this case to the circumstances which were being considered by the Court of Appeal and the House of Lords in Vine Vs. The National Dock Labour Board. There the plaintiff was working under a Code which had statutory powers and clearly in those circumstances, all the Lords of Appeal who dealt with the case in the House of Lords took the view that the case could not be dealt with as though it were an ordinary master and servant claim in which the right of the parties are regulated solely by contract. Here despite the strong statutory flavour attaching to the plaintiff's contract, I have reached the conclusion that in essence it was an ordinary contract between master and servant and nothing more."

29. This case has been relied upon on be-half of the appellants but it does not appear that it is of much assistance to them. The memorandum issued by the Minister, the violation of the terms of which provided the cause of the said action, does not appear to have been issued under any statutory provision and as such it has not statutory force. The conditions of service in that case were considered therefore nothing more than contractual ones and the Vine's case was distinguished on that score. The employment in question may of course be considered to have a kind of public character but, as it appears from the report, no blame having been given at the time of the termination of the service, the principle of natural justice also could not be invoked.

The two Privy Council cases, viz. Francis Vs. Municipal Councillor of Kualalampur, (1962) 3 All. E. R. (P. C.) 633, and Vidyodaya University of Ceylon and others Vs. Silva (1964) 3 All. E. R. 865 may now be noticed.

30. In Francis Vs. Municipal Councillor of Kualalampur, 1962 (3) All E. R. (P. C.) 633, appellant Francis entered in 1950 in the employment of the respondent Council, and in 1953 he was taken on to their permanent staff. The Council were his employer and by virtue of section 16(5) of the Municipal Ordinance, 1948, the President had power to dismiss him. On October, 1957 the appellant was dismissed but there was irregularity and the dismissal was technically a wrongful dismissal. Since then Francis had done no work for respondent. The appellant sought a declaration that the termination of his employment was wrongful and that he had the right to continue the employment from October, 1, 1957, and alternatively he claimed damages for wrongful dismissal. The Privy Council held that when there has been a purported termination of contract of service, a declaration to the effect that the contract of service still subsisted would rarely be made, and could not be made in the absence of special circumstances because of the principle that the court could not grant specific performance of contract of service. In the present case there were no special circumstances, and the appellant's remedy lay in damages for wrongful dismissal, and the declaratory judgment sought would not be made. The Privy Council considered Vine's case but distinguished it.

31. In Vidyodaya University of Ceylon and others Vs. Silva 1964 (3) All E. R. (P. C.) 865, the facts were that by Statute establishing and regulating Vidyodaya University of Ceylon, the University by its executive body the University Council were empowered to institute professorship, and every appointment of professor was to be by agreement in writing between the University and the Professor, and was to be for such period and for such terms as the Council might resolve. By s. 18(e) of the Act of 1958 the Council had power to dismiss any officer or teacher on grounds of incapacity or conduct which in the opinion of not less than two third members of the Council, renders him unfit to be an officer or teacher of the University. The Act of 1958 did not expressly give a right of hearing, nor provide any right of appeal. The term 'Officer' included the Vice-Chancellor and the holder of any other office created by statute, and the terms 'teacher' included a professor, lecturer or other person imparting instruction. By letter dated September 1, 1960, the respondent pursuant to the Council's decision, was appointed professor and Head of the Department of Economics and Business Administration at the University, and by letter dated September 2, 1960, he accepted the appointment. He did not sign the form of agreement for use on the appointment of teacher in the University. by letter dated July 4, 1961 the respondent was informed by the Vice-Chancellor that at a meeting of the Council held that day, it had been unanimously resolved to terminate his appointment from that day. The respondent sought a writ certiorari to quash the Council's order dismissing him, on the ground that the Council were bound to act judicially in terminating his appointment and should therefore, have told him of the nature of the accusation and given him an opportunity of being heard. The Ceylon Supreme Court granted certiorari. On appeal to the Privy Council, the Board considered Vine's case among other authorities, and held that, although, the University was established and regulated by statute that did not make the contract of employment made with the teachers and subject to. S. 18(a), it Was no other than ordinary contract between master and servant; and in the present case the respondent was not shown to have any status other than that of a servant, and that the procedure by certiorari was not available where master summarily terminated servant's employment. It was held that certiorari had been wrongly granted.

32. These two Privy Council cases on which reliance has been placed by the learned Attorney-General were distinguished from Vine's case on the ground that there was no statutory element in the condition of service in these cases. It. however, appears that the dismissal of the appellant in Francis Vs. Municipal Councillors Kualalampur was under a statutory provision, namely, section 16(5) of the Municipal Ordinance, 1948 and it was admittedly irregular. Francis being an employee under the Municipal Council which was a kind of a local authority his service was of public character and under section 16(5) of the Municipal Ordinance, 1948 the President had the power to dismiss him. This power was admittedly irregularly exercised, but the prayer for a declaration that the dismissal was wrongful was refused in this case on the ground that the effect of such a declaration would be that the contract of service still subsisted and that such a declaration would be rarely made in the absence of special circumstances. It should, however, be noticed that the case was not one of a breach of contract of service and that what was sought in that case was not a specific enforcement of a contract, but a redress for a violation of a mandate of law and the prayer was for a relief against an unlawful act. When however, it is a breach of a mere term of a contract of service the specific redress against such a breach by enforcing the contract is not available to an aggrieved party.

33. It may also be pointed out, with respect, that the case of Vidyodaya University also, appears to be of doubtful validity, as it is not consistent with well known judicial principle and some distinguished English judicial authorities. There also the employment of the respondent as the Professor and Head of the Department of Economics and Business Administration of the University was taken to be a contractual one in view of the fact that the execution of a deed of permanent contract was contemplated. Under section 18(a) of the Act of 1958 under which the University was established the University Council had power to dismiss an officer or a teacher on grounds of incapacity or conduct which in the opinion of not less than two-third members of the Council render him unfit to be an officer or a teacher and under the said provision the respondent was dismissed by the Council without being given any opportunity of being heard. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council treated it to be a case of pure master and servant and as such the respondent was held to be not entitled to any declaration as to the invalidity of the order of dismissal. The decision of this case runs counter to the well established principle recognised in English Courts that any person being empowered under law to determine questions affecting the right of another person is bound to exercise that power judicially and observe the principle of natural justice.

The correctness of this decision has been doubted in a later House of Lords case of Malloch Vs. Aberdeen Corporation, to which we shall refer presently.

34. In Ridge Vs. Baldwin, 1964 A. C. 40, the House of Lords in the case of dismissal of a borough constable without show cause notice held that the dismissal was bad as the dismissed constable had a right of hearing on the principle of natural justice.

35. In 1956 the appellant Ridge was appointed Chief Constable of Borough Police Force, the appointment being subject to the Police Acts and Regulations. On October 25, 1957 he was arrested and charged, together with other persons, with conspiracy to obstruct the course of justice, On October 28, 1957, he was suspended from duty by the Borough Watch Committee. On February 28, 1958, he was acquitted by the jury on the criminal charges against him, but Donovan J. in passing sentence on two police officers who were convicted, said that the facts admitted in the course of the trial "establish that neither of you had that professional and moral leadership which both of you should have had and were entitled to expect from the Chief Constable'. On March 6, 1958, on a charge alleging corruption against the appellant, on which no evidence was offered, the judgment referred to the borough's police force and remarked on its need for a leader "who will be a new influence and who will set a different example from that which has lately obtained". After his acquittal the appellant applied to be re-instated, but on March 7, 1958, the Watch Committee at a meeting decided that he had been negligent in the discharge of his duties as Chief Constable and, in purported exercise of the powers conferred on them by section 191(4) of the Act of 1882, dismissed him from that office. No specific charge was formulated against him either at that meeting or at another on March 18, when the appellant's solicitor addressed the Committee, but the Watch Committee, in arriving at their decision, considered (inter alia) his own statements in evidence and the observations made by Donvan J. on February 28 and March 6. On the appellant's appeal to the Home Secretary, the decision given was "that there was sufficient material on which the Watch Committee could properly exercise their power of dismissal under section 191(4)." The appellant then brought an action against members of the Watch Committee for a declaration that his dismissal was illegal, ultra vires and void, and payment of salary from March 7, 1958, or alternatively, payment of pension from that date and damages. It was held that the decision of the respondents to dismiss the appellant was null and void; and that, accordingly, notwithstanding that the decision of the Home Secretary was "final and binding on the parties" by section 2(3) of the Police Appeals Act, 1927, that decision could not give validity to the decision of the respondents. The decision of the respondents was a nullity.

36. In this case the House of Lords reviewed a number of authorities on the question whether a body of persons having legal authority to determine questions affecting the rights of the citizens have the duty to exercise that power judicially and after taking note of some of the recent cases in which a contrary view appears to have been expressed laid down the law in definite terms that the decision of the Watch Committee dismissing the respondent of the said case being given without observing the rule of natural justice was null and void. Lord Reid in his speech quoted with approval the following observation of Bankes L. J. as expressed in Rex Vs. Electricity Commissioners reported in (1924) 1 K. B. 171 at page 198:

"On principle and on authority it is in my opinion open to this Court to hold and I consider that it should hold, that powers so far reaching affecting as they do individuals as well as property are powers to be exercised judicially and not ministerially or merely, to use the language of Pallas C. B., as proceedings towards legislation."

and proceeded to give his own view (with which all the Law Lords excepting Lord Ever-shed agreed) in the following manner :-

"Time and again in the cases I have cited it has been stated that a decision given without regard to the principles of natural justice is void I see no reason to doubt these authorities. The body with the power to decide cannot lawfully proceed to make a decision until it has afforded to the person affected a proper opportunity to state his case."

<u>37. It is interesting to quote the following passage at page 108 of the Report from the concurring speech delivered in this case by Lord Morris of Borth Gest who appears to have expressed somewhat different views in the case of the Vidyodaya University Vs. Silva and also in another case, viz. Matlock Vs. Abardeen Corporation (1971) 1 W.L.R. 1578 same case (1971) 2 All. E. R. 1278 to which we will presently refer:</u>

<u>"In my judgment once there was a report or allegation from which it appeared that a Chief Constable might have committed an offence, it was a condition precedent to any dismissal based on a finding of guilt of such offence that the Regulations should in essentials have been put into operation. They included and incorporated the principles of natural justice which, as Haman L. J. (1962 (1) All. E. R. at p. 850) said, only fair play in action. It is well established that the essential requirements on natural justice at least include that before someone is condemned he is to have an opportunity of defending himself and that in order that he may do so he is to be made aware of the charges of allegations or suggestions which he has to meet: See Kanada Vs. Government of Federation of Malaya. (1962 A. C. 322). My Lords, here is something which is basic to our system; the importance of upholding it far transcends the significance of any particular case."</u>

<u>38. The noble Lord, of course, tried to distinguish the said case from a master and servant case by observing that the appellant held in office from which the Watch Committee could at any time dismiss him if they thought that he had been negligent in the dis-charge of his duty, but the fact remains that what was sought to be terminated was a kind of contract of service, and he proceeded to add at page 109 of the Report.</u>

<u>"Being of the view that even if there had been no applicable regulations a decision to dismiss the appellant for neglect of duty ought only to have been taken in the exercise of a quasi judicial function which demanded observance of the rules of natural justice."</u>

39. We have referred to the observation of Bankes L. J. made in Rex Vs. Electricity Commissioner, as quoted by Lord Reid in Ridge Vs. Baldwin, in which the duty of exercising a power judicially was inferred from the nature of the power itself. Lord Reid appears to have made a very close examination of a number of the past authorities in Ridge Vs. Baldwin in order to show that the view expressed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Nakkuda Ali Vs. Jayaratne (1951) A. C. 66 to the effect that the duty of exercising a power judicially is dependent not only on the nature of the power but also on the requirement of it by positive law was not in accord with the old authorities and was also based on a misunderstanding of the dictum of Lord Atkin, as expressed in Rex Vs. Electricity .Commissioner, and a gloss put on it by Lord Hewart C. J. in Rex Vs. Legislative Committee of the Churche Assembly (1928) 1 K. B. 411.

40. The House of Lords had again to consider the question of master and servant in the case of Malloch Vs. Aberdeen Corporation (1971) 1 W.L.R. 1578 which is a recent case of the House of Lords. The facts were that in August, 1965 the appellant entered the employment of an education authority as a teacher qualified by certification. In March 1969 the Education Committee, to whom the authority its power, passed a resolution to dismiss him and notice of dismissal was served on him by a letter. The ground of dismissal was that, since he was not registered in terms of paragraph 2 of Schedule 2 to the Regulation made under section 2(1) of the Education (Scotland) Act 1956 and the amending Regulation 4(2) of the Schools (Scotland) Code 1956, his continued employment would have been unlawful in an action against the education authority he claimed that the purported dismissal was a nullity because : (1) it was contrary to natural justice, since he was not given a hearing and (2) the resolution was passed under an error of law, since the Committee had a discretion in the matter which it had failed to exercise. The prayer was al-lowed. On the question of applicability of the natural justice rule, it was held that denial of hearing to the appellant was a breach of duty of the Committee.

41. It is to be noticed that under the Education (Scotland) Act, 1872, every appointment of a teacher was to be during the pleasure of the School Board and it was held in Morrison Vs. Abernathy School Board (1876) 3 R 945 that the position of a teacher after the said Act was that of an ordinary master and servant under the common law. Thereafter the Public Schools (Scotland Teachers Act, 1882 was passed providing that no certificated teacher should be dismissed without due notice to him and without due deliberation on the part of the School Board and also laying down regulatory procedure as to how a resolution of an education authority for the dismissal of such a teacher should be passed. The present Education (Scotland) Act, 1962 contain similar provisions as to an appointment being during the pleasure of the appointing education authority and also as to the procedure regulating dismissal, which was continued in force in a varied and amplified form. In 1967, certain regulations were made under the authority of the Education Act providing that every teacher employed by an education authority should be registered. Malloch, who was a certificated teacher, as required under the previous law, i refused to register on the idea that the new law was not attracted in the case of the old employees. The education authority however, being advised that they had no option but to dismiss the appellant adopted a resolution to dismiss him and gave the appellant a notice of dismissal. The ground on which this resolution was challenged was that, contrary to natural justice, the committee refused to receive written representation or to afford to the appellant hearing before the authority passed this resolution, although the notice as required under the Education Act was given. Lord Reid again (Lord Morris and Lord Guest dissenting and Lord Wilberforce and Lord Simon concurring) expressed his view in the following at page 1282 of the report:

"An elected public body is in a very different position from a private employer. Many i of its servants in the lower grades are in the same position as servants of a private employer. Butmany in higher grades or offices are given special statutory status or protection. The right of a man to be heard in his own defence is the most elementary protection of all and, where a statutory form of protection would be less effective if it did not carry with it a right to be heard, I would not find it difficult to imply this right."

As regards the question as to the legal bar against the specific enforcement of a contract of personal service, the following observation of Lord Reid at page 1284 is important:

"It was argued that it would not be right to reduce the resolution of dismissal because that would involve the reinstatement of the appellant in effect granting specific implement of his contract of employment which the law does not permit. But that would not the effect. There would be no reinstatement. The result would be to hold that the appellant's contract of employment had never been terminated and. it would be open to the respondents at any time hereafter to dismiss him if they chose to do so and did so in lawful manner. Unless they chose to do that the appellant's contract of employment would continue. Then it was said that the proper remedy would be damages. But in my view if an employer fails to take the preliminary steps which the law regards as essential he has no power to dismiss and any purported dismissal is a nullity. We were not referred to any case where a dismissal after failure to afford a hearing which the law required to be afforded was held to be anything but null and void."

42. Lord Morris and Lord Guest who dissented from the majority view proceeded mainly on the basis that the relevant statute having referred to the appointment of a teacher being during the pleasure of the appointing authority and the procedure laid down for the adoption of a resolution of dismissal having not expressly required that an opportunity of being heard should be given to the teacher concerned there was no obligation on the part of the education authority to afford such an opportunity to the teacher.

<u>43. Lord Wilberforce delivered a very illuminating speech in this case which is very helpful for finding out the basic principle which underlies the distinction between a pure master and servant case and a case where the principles and remedies of administrative law are applicable. We can usefully quote the following passage from his speech:</u>

<u>"The argument that once it is shown that the relevant relationship is that of master and servant, this is sufficient to exclude the requirements of natural justice is often found, in one form or another, in reported cases. There are two reasons behind it. The first is that, in master and servant cases, one is normally in the field of the i common law of contract inter parties, so that principles of administrative law, including those of natural justice, have no part to play, The second relates to the remedy : it is that in pure master and servant cases, the most that can be obtained is damages, if the dismissal is wrongful; no order for reinstatement can be made, so no room exists for such remedies as administrative law may grant, such as a declaration that the dismissal is void. I think, there is validity in both of these arguments, but they, particularly the first, must be carefully used. It involves the risk of compartmental approach which, although convenient as a solvent, may lead to narrower distinctions than are appropriate to the broader issues of administrative law. A comparative list of the situations in which persons have been held entitled or not entitled to a hearing or to observation of rules of natural justice, according to the master and servant test, looks illogical and even bizzarre. A specialist surgeon is denied protection which is given to a hospital doctor; a University professor, as a servant, has been denied the right to be heard, a dock labourer and an undergraduate have been granted it; example's can be multiplied (See Barber Vs. Manchester Regional Hospital Board (1958 1 All. E. R. 322, Palmer Vs. Inverness Hospitals Board (1963 SC 311), Vidyodaya University of Ceylon Vs. Silva, (1964) 3 All. E. R. 65, Vine Vs. National Dock Labour Board, (1957 A. C. 488), Glynn Vs. Keele University, (1971) 1 W.L.R. 487. One may accept that if there are relationships in which all requirements of the observance of rules of natural justice are excluded (and I do not wish to assume that this is inevitably so) these must be confined to what have been called pure master and servant cases, which I take to mean cases in which there is no element of public employment or service, no support by statute, nothing in the nature of an office or a status which is capable of protection. If any of these elements exist, then in my opinion whatever the terminology used, even though in some inter parties aspects the relationship may be called that of master and servant, there may be essential procedural requirements to be observed, and failure to observe them may result in a dismissal being declared to be void.</u>

<u>" Having regard to the principle as laid down in the above passage, the noble Lord failed to appreciate the propriety of the decision given in the case of The Vidyodaya University of Ceylon Vs. Silva and pointed out in his speech in the following words, the basic character of the relationship which called for an appropriate remedy of administrative law but was denied by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council:</u>

<u>…..there are some cases where the distinction has been lost sight of, and where the mere allocation of the label—master and servant—has been thought decisive against an administrative law remedy. One such, which I refer to because it may be thought to have some relevance here, is Vidyodaya University of Ceylon Vs. Silva, concerned with a University professor, who was dismissed without a hearing. He succeeded before the Supreme Court of Ceylon in obtaining an order for certiorari to quash the decision of the University, but the judgment was set aside by the Privy Council on the ground that the relation was that of master and servant to which the remedy of certiorari had no application. It would not be necessary or appropriate to disagree with the procedural or even the factual basis on which the decision rests; but I must confess that I could not follow it in this country in so far as it involves a denial of any remedy of administrative law to analogous employments. Statutory provisions similar to those on which the employment rested would tend to show, to my mind, in England or in Scotland, that it was one of sufficiently public character or one partaking sufficiently of the nature of an office, to attract appropriate remedies of administrative law."</u>

44. Learned Attorney-General has relied very much upon the Queen's Bench Decision in the case of Barber Vs. Manchester Regional hospital Board and the two decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Francis Vs. Municipal Councillors, Kualalampur and Vidyodaya University of Ceylon Vs. Silva. As it has already been pointed out, the Barber's case can be distinguished inasmuch as it does not appear from the report that the Memorandum issued by the Minister the violation of which was the basis of Barber's complaint had any statutory force or there was any question of denial of natural justice. But the two Privy Council decisions referred to undoubtedly lend some kind of support to the contention of the appellants in these two. It should however be mentioned that these decisions do not appear to be consistent with the principles laid down in the three House of Lords cases noticed above, viz., Vine Vs. National Dock Labour Board, Ridge Vs. Bald-win and Malloch Vs. Aberdeen Corporation. Lord Wilberforce, in his speech in Malloch's case, rather considered the decisions in the Barber's case and Vidyodaya University's case, "`illogical and even bizarre" and the noble Lord, as we have seen, proceeded to examine specifically the Vidyodaya University's case and expressed an opinion that such a decision should not be followed in England and Scotland.

<u>45. It is no doubt true that the English decisions have not been uniform, and sometimes they appear to be perplexing but the distinguished opinion which has been so lucidly expressed in those important decisions of the House of Lords in expounding in an illuminating way the position of an employee of a statutory body having a public character has introduced a great amount of clarity and precision in the understanding of the legal right of such an employee, when excluded from his employment. The principle which has be laid down in these decisions is that when an employee holding a statutory office or having a public character, is dismissed or discharged from his employment, in contravention of a statutory provision or in violation of the principle of natural justice, he is not governed by the ordinary master and servant rule, but is entitled to appropriate relief against the order of dismissal or discharge from his employment.</u>

46. Learned Attorney General has also very strongly relied upon two recent decisions of the Indian Supreme Court, viz., Executive Committee of U. P. Warehousing Corporation Vs. Chandra Kiron Tyagi, A.I.R. 1970 S.C. 1244 and Indian Airlines Corporation Vs. Sukhedo, A.I.R. 1971 S. C. 1828 and has Contended that the regulations embodying certain conditions of service, though framed under statutory powers, are merely for the guidance of the relevant administrative authority and do not constitute any statutory restriction, the violation of which is actionable in a court of law. These decisions seem to have, as it has appeared to us, introduced an entirely new concept in the law relating to the employees of a statutory body, which is not in line with many of the distinguished judicial views of the Indian Supreme Court itself and if we may say so with great respect—does not appear to be founded on sound reasoning.

47. In the case of U. P. Warehousing Corporation, the respondent who was a ware-house man was found guilty of certain charges and dismissed from service in contravention of clause (3) of Regulation 16 of the Regulations framed by the Corporation in exercise of the powers conferred upon it by the statute under which the Corporation was established. The said clause provided that the particular punishment should not be imposed upon an employee without giving him an opportunity to tender a written explanation, to cross-examine the witnesses against him and to produce evidence in defence. It was concurrently found by all the Courts that the said provision was not complied with and the Supreme Court of India accepted the finding.

48. Facts of that case are that the Plaintiff Tyagi originally entered the service of the Warehousing Corporation as a technical assistant and later he was promoted to the post of Warehouseman, and was confirmed in the post. Certain charges were framed against Tyagi, and pending the enquiry he was suspended. Alter enquiry he was found guilty, and in consequence dismissed from the service of the Corporation. Tyagi brought a suit challenging his dismissal asserting amongst other, that the order of dismissal was in disregard of clause (16) of the Regulation framed by the Corporation. The Courts below decreed in favour of Tyagi, ordering reinstatement and holding that there was violation of Regulation 16(3) of the Corporation, and as it was a statutory rule, its violation entitled the plaintiff to a declaration of nullity. The Supreme Court of India after considering Vine's case, and a number of decisions reversed the decision of the courts below regarding' declaration of nullity and reinstatement, and held that the relevant Regulation though framed under statutory powers, will operate as terms and conditions of the service contract, and even though there was breach of the regulation, yet no declaration of nullity could be given, but it may give rise to a claim for damages only.

49. The learned Judges—they were two, Shelat and Vaidialingam, JJ—appear to have taken the view that the Regulations framed by the Corporation have no statutory force and a breach of the same does not entitle the employee to a declaration of the order made in contravention thereof to be a nullity on the reasoning that the Act does not guarantee any statutory status to the employee nor does it impose any obligation on the Corporation in such matters. Reference was made in course of the judgment to only three Indian decisions, namely, Dr. S. Dutt Vs. University of Delhi, A.I.R. 1958 S. C. 1050, S.R. Tewari Vs. District Board, Agra, A.I.R. 1964. S C. 1680, and Life Insurance Corporation of India Vs. Sunil Kumar Mukherjce, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 849 none of which dealt with the specific point on which the aforesaid view was expressed. But this view appears to have been further developed and more elaborately discussed in the subsequent case of Indian Airlines Corporation Vs. Sukhedo which was heard by a Bench of three Judges, viz. Shelat, Duo and Bhargava, JJ.

50. In that case, the respondent who was a motor driver of the Corporation was dismissed in contravention of the procedure laid down in the Regulations made by the Corporation in pursuance of a provision of the Air Corporation Act, and a declaration as to the invalidity of the said order of dismissal was given in a suit instituted by him, up to the High Court, but the Supreme Court set aside the said declaration and dismissed the employee's suit on the view as expressed below:

"The regulations contain the terms and conditions which govern the relationship between the Corporation and its employees. Though made under the power conferred by the statute, they merely embody the terms and conditions of service in the Corporation but do not constitute a statutory restriction as to the kind of contracts which the Corporation can make with its servants or the grounds on which it can terminate them. That being so and the Corporation having undoubtedly the power to dismiss its employee, the dismissal of the Respondent was with jurisdiction and although it was wrongful in the sense of its being in, breach of the terms and conditions which governed the relationship between the Corporation and the respondent it did subsist."

51. In support of the view expressed above, the learned Judge delivering the judgment of the Court has referred to a Single Judge decision of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Ram Babu Rathaur Vs. Divisional Manager, Life Insurance Corporation of India, A.I.R. 1961 All. 502 which was, according to the learned Judge, noticed with approval by the Supreme Court of India in the case of S. R. Tewari Vs. District Board, Agra, A.I.R. 1964 S. C. 1680, which again was followed by the Indian Supreme Court in the U. P. Warehousing Corporation where similar view as to the non-statutory character of a Regulation framed under a statutory power but prescribing terms and conditions of employment was expressed.

52. It may, however, be mentioned that the question whether a regulation or rule framed under statutory power but embodying conditions of service has a statutory force or not never engaged the attention of the learned Judges deciding S. R. Tewaris' case. It was argued in the said case on behalf of the District Board, the respondent, that the appellant who was an Engineer under the District Board and whose service was terminated after giving salary for three months in lieu of notice being not entitled to the protection under Article 311 of the Constitution, the jurisdiction of the High Court even under Article 226 of the Constitution was restricted by section 21(b) of the Specific Relief Act and the relief of declaration that the termination was unlawful and the consequential order for restoration in service could not be given and several decisions including the Allahabad High Court case of Rain Babu Rathaur were cited in support of the said argument. The Supreme Court of India countered this argument by observing :

"In our judgment none of these cases can be used to support the view that the High Court has no power to declare the statutory obligation of a statutory body" —The Courts are invested with the power to declare invalid the act of a statutory body, if by doing the act the body has acted in breach of a mandatory obligation imposed by statute even if by making the declaration the body is compelled to do something which it does not desire to do."

At another place of the judgment there is a reference to the aforesaid case of Ram Babu Rathaur, where it has been observed that there having been no statutory obligation imposed upon the Corporation, the High Court was right in holding in the said case that the general law of master and servant would apply. This observation appears to have been made on the assumption, as was found by the High Court, that there was no statutory provision regulating the conditions of service in the said case, without applying its mind to the question as to whether the said finding of the High Court was well reasoned or justified.
