The Supreme Court decision on the other hand proceeded to examine the facts of the case on the view that the Rule 3A framed by the State Government under section 172(2) of the District Boards Act, 1922 laying down the conditions under which the service of a permanent servant of the Board could be terminated had statutory force and required to be complied with, and ultimately disposed of the appeal by holding that the order of termination of service was lawful as the provision of Rule 3A was duly complied with.

53. We feel it necessary to refer further to the Single Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Ram Babu Rathaur as, it appears, the said case has influenced in a way the later decisions of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of the Executive Committee of the U.P. Warehousing Corporation Vs. Chandra Kiron Tyagi and the Indian Airlines Corporation Vs. Sukhdeo. In the said Allahabad case it was held that mere disregard of a Staff Regulation issued under a statutory power would not be actionable and the basis of the said decision was the two decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the cases of Rangachari Vs. Secretary of State, A.I.R. 1937 P. C. 27 and Venkata Rao Vs. Secretary of State, A.I.R. 1937 P. C. 31. which in our opinion were wrongly applied by the learned Judge of the Allahabad High Court.

54. In the said two Privy Council cases, the Judicial Committee had to consider the case of two crown servants dismissed in violation of Statutory rules and held, on the construction of section 76-B of the Government of India Act, 1919 that the service of a crown servant being at the pleasure of the sovereign and having regard to the specific provision in the said section providing that no rules or other provisions made thereunder should be construed to limit or abridge the power of the Secretary of State to deal with a civil servant, any breach of such statutory rules was not actionable in a court of law. It should be noticed that their Lordships of the Judicial Committee were not laying down a general proposition applicable to all cases of employer and employee, but they were considering the specific position of crown servants under section 76B of the Government of India Act, 1919. We do not see how these decisions could be brought in aid of the case of an employee of a Statutory Corporation.

55. In Indian Airlines Corporation Vs. Sukhdeo Rai, A.I.R. 1971 S. C. 1828, facts were, that the respondent Sukhdeo was employed as motor driver of a company, the Airways India Limited. Consequent upon the passing of the Air Corporation Act, the Indian Airlines Corporation was set up under the Act, and the respondent became an employee of the Corporation. He was dismissed from service and in a suit by him it was contended that the procedure laid down by the regulation made by the Corporation under its statutory power had not been followed. He prayed for a declaration that his dismissal was illegal and void. The trial court granted a declaration that the order dismissing the respondent was illegal and void and he continued in the service of Corporation. The Supreme Court of India on review of large number of authorities including some of the decisions above cited, held that the fact that the Corporation was set up under and regulated by a statute, would not without anything more, take away the relationship between it and its employees from the category of purely master and servant relationship, and that there is no provision in the Air Corporation Act, which imposes upon the Corporation-statutory restriction or obligation which limits its power of terminating that relationship. It was further held employment of respondent Sukhdeo not being one as an officer and there being no obligation or restriction in the Air Corporation Act, 1953 or the rules subject to which only the power to terminate could be exercised, the respondent was not entitled to a declaration that his dismissal was null and void.

56. The learned Judge of the Indian Supreme Court in delivering the judgment in the Indian Air Lines Corporation case has referred to an observation of Lord Russel in Kruse Vs. Johnson (1898) 2 Q. B. 91 in explaining the nature of a bye-law made by a County Council in pursuance of a statutory power and the said case has been cited by the learned Attorney-General also in this case in support of the proposition that the regulation embodying terms and conditions of service, even though made under a statutory power has no statutory force. We do not see how this case is of any help to the said proposition.

57. In Kruse Vs. Johnson, the validity of a bye-law, made by a County Council under a certain provision of the Local Government Act, 1888 was challenged on the ground of unreasonableness, and it was held that the bye-law in question was not bad for unreasonableness. The ground of challenge in this case appears to be novel, no doubt, as seldom a legislative enactment can be thrown out on the ground of unreasonableness, if legislative competence is there. But in case of a delegated legislation, as the said case was, the question becomes relevant in judging whether the body exercising delegated authority framed the impugned bye-law within the limits of its delegated power, as the legislature cannot be Presumed to have delegated any authority to make an unreasonable provision. It is really a question relating to ultra vires, which may be pertinent in regard to the exercise of the power of subordinate legislation.

<u>58. We have been so long trying to examine the material basis of the aforesaid two judgments of the Supreme Court of India, as given out in the said judgments, in support of their conclusion as to the non-statutory character of a regulation embodying conditions of service, even though made under a statutory power. Under the general principle of Interpretation, a delegated legislation, if properly made, and not inconsistent with any of the provision's of the parent Act or with any other provisions specified by the said Act, has got as much statutory force as the parent legislation. When a condition of service is made a subject matter of a subordinate legislation, it comes into force, not by virtue of a bilateral contract between the parties but by virtue of the said legislative enactment. Whether a particular term of service is contractual or statutory is dependent upon the facts of each case. There is nothing inherently contractual in a term of service in the sense that it cannot shed off this character even if it is made a part of a regulation having the force of law. The Supreme Court of India appears to have consistently accepted this position with regard to the rules and regulations framed under statutory powers until the said two decisions in the cases of the U. P. Ware-housing Corporation and the Indian Airlines Corporation, which have tried to formulate an entirely new concept.</u>

59. In the case of Life Insurance Corporation of India and others Vs. Sunil Kumar Mukherjee and others reported in A.I.R. 1964. S. C. 849, the Supreme Court of India had to examine the validity and comparative efficacy of different kinds of subordinate legislations. Udder the Life Insurance Corporation Act, the employee's of various Insurance Companies became the employees of the newly set up Corporation on the same terms and conditions as they had as employees under the said Companies unless and until their employments were terminated or until their terms and conditions were duly altered by the Corporation. Government issued an Order under section 11 of the Act, clause (10) of which provided that in case of unsatisfactory performance, misconduct, negligence etc. the service of an employee might be terminated after giving him an opportunity of showing cause against action proposed to be taken against him. Under section 49 of the Act the Corporation had the power to frame Regulations, and one of clauses of the Regulations framed by the Corporation prescribed that in judging a Field Officer's work, the Corporation should observe the principle contained in the circular issued by the Managing Director and the said circular provided, inter aria, that in case poor performance etc. the services of the Field officers would be terminated. The Corporation terminated the services of the respondents by an order without giving them any prior notice, Respondents contention was that the order of termination was bad as they were not given any opportunity to show cause against the action taken against them, as was clearly provided in clause (10) of the Government Order made under section 11 of the Act. The Corporation's contention on the other hand was that under para 4(a) of the circular issued under clause (11) of the Government Order such kind of termination was provided. It was held in the said case that the procedure laid down in clause (10) of the Government Order could not be superseded by a circular issued under a Regulation framed under section 49 read with clause (11) of the Order and that as such the order of termination made in violation of the Government order was invalid. Gajendragadkar, J (as he then was), with whom Wanchoo and Das Gupta JJ concurred, in explaining the legal position about the character of the relevant statutory provisions made the following observation:

"It is plain that the provisions contained in section 11(2) of the Act are paramount and would over-ride any contrary provisions contained in the Order or Regulations. Subject to the provisions of section 11(2), the provisions of the Order will prevail, because the Order has been issued by the Central Government by virtue of the powers conferred on it by section 11(2) itself. The provisions of the Order in law partake of the character of the rules framed under section 48 of the Act. Thus next to the provisions of section 11(2) of the Act will stand the provisions of the Order. Then we have the Regulations issued by the Corporation under section 49(1) of the Act. But it must be borne in mind that the power of the Corporation to make the Regulations is burdened with the conditions that these regulations must not be inconsistent with the Act and the rules framed thereunder, so that if any of the provisions contained in the Regulations made by the Corporation under section 49 are found to be inconsistent either with section 11(2) or with the Order made by the Central Government under section 11(2) would be invalid. It is in the light of this legal position that the problem posed before us in the present appeals must be decided."

60. We thus find that according to the learned Judges of the said case, a Regulation framed by the Corporation relating to conditions of service has undoubtedly a statutory force subject to the condition that it must not be inconsistent with the provisions of the parent Act or with any of the rules framed under the said Act In the case of Indian Air Lines Corporation, it was observed, in seeking to distinguish the aforesaid case of Life Insurance Corporation of India, that the decision in the latter case which was based on different facts and on different principles could not be legitimately invoked by the respondents. With great respect we may say that we have been unable to notice the distinction, so far as the basic principle is concerned.

61. Mafatlal Narandas Barat Vs. J. D. Rakbod , Divisional Collector State Transport and another, in A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 1364 is another case of the Indian Supreme Court, which was decided by a Bench of five Judges on the view that a Regulation framed by the State Transport Corporation regarding the conditions of service of the employees of the Corporation had a statutory character and that an order of termination of the service of an employee in violation of the provision of such a Regulation was invalid. It was also held that the order of termination of the service was bad because of violation of the principle of natural justice as well. Gajendragadkar, C. J. with whom Wanchoo, Hidayatullah, Rameswami and Satyanarayana Raju JJ. concurred, in giving in a nutshell the main question involved in the case, made the following observation at page 1365 of the report:

"It may be stated at the outset that the respondent is an autonomous statutory Corporation formed under the provisions of the Road Transport Corporation Act, 1950, It is not disputed that the appellant could not invoke the provision of Article 311 of the Constitution. The short question for determination in the appeal is whether the appellant was entitled to an opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment as required by Regulation No. 61 of the Regulations which govern the service conditions of the employees of the Corporation."

and the learned Chief Justice gave the decision of the Court at page 1366 of the Report in the following words:

"The order of termination passed against the appellant is bad in law since it contravenes the provisions of clause 4(b) of the Regulations and also the principle of natural justice."

62. The learned Judges deciding the Indian Airlines Corporation case, however, thought it wise to ignore the aforesaid decisions of the Indian Supreme Court to which some of the eminent Judges of the said Court were parties, on the following reasoning:

"But the question whether the said Regulations constituted a t the obligation subject to which only the power to terminate employment could be exercised or not, or the question whether they took the employment out of master and servant relationship was not canvassed. Neither the decision in S. R. Tewari's case (A.I.R. 1964 S. C. 1680) nor any other similar decision was also, it seems, brought to the notice of the Court."

63. As we have noticed, both in the Life Insurance Corporation of India case (A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 847) as well as Mafatlal Narandas Barat case (A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 1364) the Courts concerned proceeded to decide the cases on the view that a Regulation framed by a Corporation in exercise of the statutory power conferred on it by a competent legislature was a kind of legislation, though subordinate in character in the sense that it should not be inconsistent with any of the provisions of the parent Act or any of the rules framed thereunder and that subject to the aforesaid limitation a Regulation was binding as a statutory provision on all concerned including the administrative authority. It is an accepted concept of the constitutional law that a competent law making body which has derived its powers from the sovereign has the authority to delegate its own legislative power to another body by enacting a statute enabling thereby the said body to make rules, regulations, bye-laws etc. for the purpose of carrying out the object of the said statute and that the said body acting under the delegated authority exercises the same law-making power as belongs to the sovereign. We may usefully quote here the following statement made in the Halsbury's Laws of England (3rd Edition) Vol. 36 at pages 476-477 on the subject of Delegated Legislation:

"Subordinate legislation is legislation made by a person or body other than the sovereign in Parliament by virtue of powers conferred either by statute or by legislation which is itself made under statutory powers. It is frequently referred as delegated legislation in the former case, and sub-delegated legislation in the latter.

In volume, though not in significance, subordinate legislation is today unequalled by any other branch of written law. Much of it is made by executive authorities, the granting of powers to whom was long ago accepted by Parliament as inevitable in cases of national emergency, where speedier remedies are called for than it is itself able to provide and since Parliament has neither the time nor in all cases, sufficiently expert knowledge itself to formulate all the matters of detail with which modern legislation must be concerned has now come to regarded as a day to day inevitability. Much subordinate legislation, on the other hand, is made by independent persons and bodies to whom Parliament has entrusted the responsibility for, or the privilege of, regulating specified matters, whichever may be the case, such legislation has, if validly made, the full force and effect of a statute; but it differs from a statute in that its validity whether as i respects from or substance is normally open to challenge in the courts."

And the following statement at pages 484-485 further elucidates the character of a subordinate legislation:

"Subordinate legislation has, if validly made, the full force and effect of a statute, and this is so whether or not the statute under which it is made provides expressly that it is to have effect as if enacted therein. Thus, if an instrument made in the exercise of delegated powers directs or forbids the doing of a particular thing, the result of a breach thereof is, in the absence of provision to the contrary, the same, as if the command in prohibition had been contained in the enabling statutes itself. Similarly, if such an instrument authorises or requires the doing of any act, the principles to be applied in determining whether a person injured by the act has any right of action in respect of the injury, are no different from those applicable where damage results from an act done under the direct authority of a statute.

<u>64. The following statement in Craies on Statute Law, 6th Edition (1963) at page 289 is also to be same effect:</u>

<u>"In addition to the common law and statute law, the law of the land includes a great deal of what may be termed subordinate or "delegated" legislation. It comprises Orders in Council, departmental orders, rules, regulations, schemes, bye-laws etc. made under statutory powers"</u>

<u>No contrary considerations of Constitutional Law have been suggested in the later two Indian decisions, which not being noticed, it may have been argued, have detracted from the authority of the earlier two decisions of the same Court. The other ground stated for not accepting the authority of the earlier decision in the case of Mafatial Narandas Barat is that the attention of the Court deciding that case was not drawn to the decision in S.R. Tewari's case and similar other decisions. We have already noticed that no question relating to the statutory effect of rules or regulations embodying conditions of service was raised or considered in S.R. Tewari's case. The learned Judges in the said case rather appear to have proceeded on the view that Rule 3A framed by the District Board and laying down the manner of termination of the service of its employees had statutory force and the enquiry in the said case was confined to the consideration whether in terminating the service of the appellant the procedure laid down in the said Rule was violated. Our attention has not been drawn to any other authoritative Indian or other decisions where a view has been taken to the effect that a regulation framed by a statutory body in exercise of the legislative power conferred upon it, relating to the terms and conditions of employment shall, notwithstanding its statutory origin, be deemed to be mere contractual term or condition.</u>

65. Reference was, of course, also made in both the later two decisions of the Indian Supreme Court to the case of Dr. S. Dutt Vs. University of 1958 S.C. 1050, where it was observed that when an award held that a Professor of the University had been dismissed wrongfully and malafide, that the dismissal had no effect on his status and that he still continued to be a Professor of the University, it directed specific enforcement of a contract of personal service and as such was clearly erroneous. This case assumed that there was no element involved in that case other than that of breach of a contract of personal service. As a matter of fact, in repelling a contention made on behalf of the appellant on the basis of the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case, The High Commissioner for India Vs. I.M. Dall 75 Ind. App. 225 same case A.I.R. 1948 P.C. 121, the learned Judges of the Supreme Court of India observed that all that the Judicial Committee did in that case was to make a declaration of a statutory invalidity of an act, which was a thing entirely different from enforcing a contract of personal service. This case, thus we see, had nothing to do with the character or import of a subordinate legislation like a Regulation. We must, however, observe, as it has occurred to us, that in the said case of the Delhi University the full attention of the Court was not paid to the other aspect of the matter to which we shall presently revert. The Single Judge decision of the Allahabad High Court is of course an exception, but we have already seen that the said decision is founded on a wrong premise.

66. We have given our serious consideration to the said two Indian decisions on which strong reliance has been placed by the learned Attorney-General, but we regret to say, with respect, that we are unable to accept the proposition laid down in the said two cases to be correct, and are definitely of the view that a regulation relating to the terms and conditions of service, framed by a statutory body in exercise of the legislative powers conferred upon it, if made within the ambit of such power, has statutory force and the violation of such a regulation may, in an appropriate case, be a nullity.

<u>67. We have already noticed the principle requiring an administrative body to decide certain matters in a judicial manner , as was explained in Ridge Vs. Baldwin, 1964 A.C. 40 and before we close our discussion on the Indian cases, we shall refer to two more Indian cases, in this connection, viz, State of Orissa Vs. Dr. Miss Binapani Dai, A.I.R. 1967 S.C. 1269 and Dr. Bool Chand Vs. Chancellor, Kurilkshetra University, A.I.R. 1968 S.C. 292 in which the said principle, if we may say so with respect, was correctly enunciated.</u>

68. The case of The State of Orissa Vs. Dr. Miss Binapani Dai was a case of a disputed date of birth of the respondent and the Govt. of Orissa, after holding an enquiry re-fixed her date of birth and retired her on the basis thereof. The question was whether the enquiry was properly held, and the Supreme Court of India held that the enquiry and the decision therein were contrary to the basic concept of justice and could not have any value.

69. Shah, J. with Mitter, J concurring, made the following statement of law in the said case at page 1271 of the report:

"The rule that a party to whose prejudice an order is intended to be passed is entitled to a hearing applies alike to judicial tribunals and bodies of persons invested with authority to adjudicate upon matters involving civil consequences. It is one of the fundamental rules of our constitutional set up that every citizen is protected against exercise of arbitrary authority by the State or its Officers. Duty to act judicially would therefore arise from the very nature of the function intended to be performed; it need not be shown to be super added. If there is power to decide and determine to the prejudice of a person, duty to act judicially is implicit in the exercise of such power. If the essentials of justice be ignored and an order to the prejudice of a person is made, the order is a nullity. This is a basic concept of the rule of law and importance thereof transcends the significance of a decision in any particular case."

<u>70. This principle was followed in the case of Dr. Bool Chand Vs. The Chancellor, Kurukshetra University, where the validity of an order terminating the service of the appellant from the office of the Vice-Chancellor was challenged. The office of the Vice-Chancellor being created by a statute, the Supreme Court of India formulated the law in the judgment of the case in the following words at page 197 of the report:</u>

<u>"The University Act, the Statutes and Ordinances do not lay down the conditions in which the appointment of the Vice-Chancellor may be determined; nor does the Act prescribe any limitations upon the exercise of the power of the Chancellor to determine the employment. But once the appointment is made in pursuance of a statute, though the appointing authorty is not precluded from determining the employment the decision of the appointing authority to terminate the appointment may be based only upon the result of an enquiry held in a manner consistent with the basic concept of justice and fair play."</u>

<u>After referring to the case of Ridge Vs. Baldwin the learned Judges of the Supreme Court took the view that the case of the Vice-Chancellor fell within the third class of dismissal mentioned by Lord Reid and the tenure of his office therefore could not be interrupted without first informing him of what was alleged against him and without giving him an opportunity to make his defence or explanation. It was of course held in that case on merits that there was no violation of the said principle as enunciated above and that, therefore, no exception could be taken to the order of termination of the service of the appellant.</u>

<u>71. It may be pointed out that the case of Dr. S. Dutt Vs. University of Delhi does not appear to have been tested from the stand point of the principle referred to in the cases of The State of Orissa Vs. Dr. Miss Binapani Dei and Dr. Bool Chand Vs. The Chancellor, Kurukshetra University. Had it been so, the finding of the arbitrator, Prof. Shaba, that Dr. Dutt was wrongfully dismissed, that his dismissal was ultra vires, malafide and had no effect on his status and that he still continued to be a professor of the University, could not have been found to be erroneous on the face of it.</u>

72. Before we refer to the decisions of the Pakistan Supreme Court relating to the employees of a statutory body it is necessary to take notice here of these decisions of the said Court where the circumstances requiring the application of the principle of natural justice have been explained, as the principle of natural justice has a great bearing upon the rights of an employee serving a statutory corporation of a public character.

73. The first important decision on the question is the case of Tariq Transport Company Vs. Sargodha:-Bhera Bus Service reported in 11 D.L.R. (S.C.) 140 same case P.L.D. 1958 S.C. Pak . 437, where Munir C.J. while examining the limits of judicial review of the administrative acts enunciated the rule in the following words:

“……..at present the rule appears to be that the proceedings before an inferior tribunal, whatever be its general character, are liable to be controlled by the High Court if the law by which it is governed makes it an essential condition of its jurisdiction to find the facts which require or empower it to make an order and the order actually made adversely affects the rights of a party."

74. A writ was refused in the above-mentioned case on the ground that it was impossible to hold that the Regional Transport Authority acts judicially when it grants or refuses a permit or accepts or rejects a representation. No exception can be taken to the view, as the Transport Authority did not purport, by such action, to affect any existing right or advantage of the respondent, but had it been a case of cancellation of a permit held by the respondent the position might have been different, as actually arose in the case of M/s. Faridsons Ltd. Vs. Govt. of Pakistan 13 D.L.R. (S.C.) 233 same case P.L.D. 1961 S.C. 537, to which we shall presently refer.

75. The next case where the Supreme Court of Pakistan had to consider the rule of natural justice was the case of the Chief Commissioner, Karachi Vs. Mrs. Dina Sohrab Khatrak reported in 11 D.L.R. (S.C.) 113 same case P.L.D. 1959 S.C. 45 and Shahabuddin, J (as he then was) stated the rule in the following term:

"It cannot be disputed that it is a principle of natural justice that no one shall be dealt with to his material disadvantage or deprived of his liberty or property without having an opportunity of being heard and making his defence ." and the learned Judge proceeded to add:

“…..the above rule of justice is not confined to proceedings before courts but extends to all proceedings by whomsoever held which may affect the person or property or other right of the parties concerned in the dispute. As a just decision in such controversies is possible only if the parties are given the opportunity of being heard, there can be, as regards the right of hearing, no difference between the proceedings which are strictly judicial and those which are in the nature of a judicial proceeding though administrative in form."

76. In the case of Messrs Faridsons Ltd. Vs. Government of Pakistan, the Import Registration Certificates of the two appellants were suspended and one of the appellants was debarred from getting any Export Registration Certificate, by the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports without giving any opportunity of being heard. The West Pakistan High Court, Karachi Bench, dismissed the application of the appellants for a writ on the view that the Chief Controller was not required by law to act judicially and that the rule of natural justice which was based on certain English precedents had no application to Pakistan which was wholly governed by statute law. On appeal from the said decision, the Supreme Court of Pakistan reversed the said view and it was pointed out that in Mrs. Dina Sohrab Khatrak's case it had already been laid down by the Pakistan Supreme Court that the maxim, audi alteram partem 'No man shall be condemned unheard' applied to all judicial or administrative bodies, specially where the proceedings taken may affect the person or property or other rights of the parties concerned in the dispute. The Tariq Transport Company's case was distinguished on the footing that no private rights were involved in the matters coming up for decision before the Transport Authority which was to decide in accordance with what they conceived to be larger public interest. It was, however, noticed in the judgment of S.A. Rahman, J delivered in Messrs Faridsons Ltd.'s case that the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council expressed a view in Nakhuda Ali Vs. Jayratne (1951) A.C. 66 to the effect that it was not enough that a body should have legal authority to determine a question affecting the rights of the subject, but that there must be super added to it a duty `to act judicially' and the learned Judge appears to have clearly dissented from the said view of the Judicial Committee by observing that it "seems to run counter to a long line of English decision in the English Courts, extending back for more than a century, in "which administrative decisions affecting individuals rights and liberties were quashed if the party concerned had not been given a fair opportunity to make objection. We have already noted that the House of Lords expressed the same view in Ridge Vs. Baldwin as Mr. Justice S.A. Rahman in respect of the view of the Judicial Committee in Nakhuda Ali Vs. Jayratne.

77. In the case of Dacca University Vs. Zakir Ahmed, 16 D.L.R. (S.C.) 722 same case P.L.D. 1964 S.C. Pakistan Supreme Court gave further consideration to the principle of natural justice in connection with the case of a student expelled from the University on the charge of misconduct in the examination hall without giving the said student any opportunity of explanation, and the law stated by Hamoodur Rahman, J (as he then was) in the following words:

"From a careful review of the decisions cited before us it appears that where any person or body of persons is empowered to take decisions after ex post facto investigation into facts which would result in consequences affecting the person, property or other right of another person, then in the absence of any express words in the enactment giving such power excluding the application of the principles of natural justice, the Courts of law are inclined generally to imply that the power so given is coupled with a duty to act in accordance with such principles of natural justice as may be applicable in the facts and circumstances of given case."

<u>78. The same view was reiterated in the case of A. Saboer Khan Vs. Karachi University. 18 D.L.R. (S.C.) 422, by S.A. Rahman, J, (as he then was) in delivering the judgment of the Bench as follows:</u>

<u>"No one can be condemned unheard is one of the settled principles of law, and such a principle will be read into the relevant law,  unless its application is excluded by express words. A duty is cast upon every administrative tribunal to act with due regard to the principles of natural justice, unless specifically exempted from such a limitation. Mere omission from the relevant law, of a provision for notice, would not affect his position.''</u>

79. We thus find that Pakistan Supreme Court clearly laid down in course of several authoritative pronouncements that whenever a person or a body of persons is invested with a legal authority to determine a question affecting the rights of another, his authority is coupled with a duty of acting judicially and of observing the principle of natural justice as required by the facts of a particular case.

80. We have been called upon to decide in these appeals how far the said requirement of judicial manner of disposal and observance of the rule of natural justice can be invoked in respect of an order of dismissal of an employee of a statutory body an administrative functionary of such a body. We have also been addressed on the question whether, and to what extent, the case of an employee of a statutory body dismissed in violation of a statutory rule or procedure, is lifted out of a master and servant rule.

<u>81. The first case of an employee of a statutory body considered by the Pakistan Supreme Court was the case of The Lahore Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. Vs. Pir Saif Ullah Shah, 12 D.L.R. S.C. 108 same case P.L.D. 1959 S.C. 310, where it was held that the respondent, the Commercial Manager of the appellant Bank, who was dismissed on charges of misconduct, was not entitled to a writ of mandamus for restoration to his office in the Bank which was a private Corporation. It was accepted in the said case, relying upon the English principles; that it was a sound proposition of law that a person holding an office of public nature from which he had been wrongfully dismissed was entitled to the relief, by an order of appropriate writ, of restoration to his office. Although the nature and function of the Co-operative Bank concerned was not analysed, the Supreme Court of Pakistan took the said Bank to be a private corporation, and held that the relationship between the said Bank and the respondent was no more than that of an ordinary master and servant. It was also held in the said case that the Civil Service Rules which was adopted by the Managing Committee by a resolution and the violation of which was complained of in respect of the passing of the impugned order of dismissal, did not acquire any statutory force and as such the order of dismissal, even if passed in contravention of the said Rules, was not actionable.</u>

82. The question as to the observance of the rare of natural justice was raised in the case of Faiz Ahmed Vs. Registrar, Co-operative Societies, West Pakistan reported in 14 D.L.R. S.C. 183 same case P.L.D. 1962 S.C. 315 where the appellant, a Cashier of a Branch Office of the Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. was dismissed from his service on various charges after an enquiry had been held in regard to the said Charges. It was contended, inter alia, that the enquiry had been vitiated on account of the failure of the Enquiry Officer to follow the principles of natural justice and the High Court having dismissed the appellant's petition for an appropriate writ summarily, leave was granted by the Pakistan Supreme Court to consider whether the rule of natural justice was complied with, in so far as opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses on whose testimony the Enquiry Officer relied had been denied to the appellant. The Supreme Court, on a consideration of the records of the case, was satisfied that there was no violation of the principle of natural justice in that case. This case has been decided on the assumption, which does not appear to have been disputed, that the Principle of natural justice is attracted to the case of dismissal of an employee of a statutory body and the position of such an employee is outside the ambit of the master and servant rule.

83. In the case of Managing Committee of Co-operative Model Town Society Ltd. Vs. service e Kb. Mohammad Iqbal, reported in (1963) 15 DLR SC 116—PLD 1963 SC 179 a writ was issued at the instance of the respondent ,whose v the Secretary of the Co-operative Model Town Society Ltd. was terminated by a resolution adopted by the Managing Committee of the said Co-operative Society; directing that a duly constituted Appellate Board should hear and decide the appeal of the respondent against his dismissal. The earlier case of The Lahore Central Co-operative Bank Vs. Saifullah Shah was distinguished on the grounds firstly, that the respondent in the later case held, as the Secretary to a Co-operative Society, a statutory office within the Co-operative Societies Act, whereas the respondent in the earlier case, who was a Commercial Manager, did not hold such a statutory office and secondly, that the Society in the later case exercised administrative function in a considerable township, viz Model Town, implying perhaps thereby that the Society in question had a sufficiently public character.

84. In the case of Zainul Abedin Vs. Multan Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. Multan reported in 18 DLR (SC) 462 same case PLD 1966 SC 445, the Supreme Court of Pakistan took a view that for the purpose of restoration to office a writ of mandamus was not available to the appellant, who as an Accountant of the Co-operative Bank was dismissed from the service of the said Bank on the grounds of, inter-alia, want of necessary qualification and actions detrimental to the interest of the institution. An appeal was filed against the order of dismissal (as not being) in accordance with the Civil Service Rules as adopted by the respondent Bank, to the Commissioner of Development, who allowed the appeal on the view that no reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken was given to the employee concerned, as required under the Civil Service Rules, and set aside the order of the Registrar Co-operative Societies under whose directive the order of termination was issued by the Bank. This order was communicated to the Bank by the Commissioner, Co-operative Societies, West Pakistan, but the Bank having refused to implement the Government order and reinstate the appellant, the High Court was moved in its writ jurisdiction, but it rejected the appellant's application summarily. On appeal, the Supreme Court having held that there was no statutory duty cast upon the Bank requiring it to carry out the appellate orders of the Government made under the Act on the rules framed thereunder and that the office of an Accountant of a Co-operative Bank was not one of public nature, did not consider it a proper case where the writ of Mandamus should issue. It is not necessary for our present purpose to see whether the Supreme Court of Pakistan was correct in view that there was no statutory duty cast upon the Bank to comply with an order made by the Government under the Act or the rules framed thereunder or that the office of an Accountant of the Bank was not an office of public nature. It is sufficient for our purpose to notice that the Supreme Court accepted the principle that if the office from which an employee has been dismissed is of public nature, the limitation of the master and servant rule cannot be invoked. It also appears that the Supreme Court accepted the principle that a writ might issue if there was contravention of a statutory provision of a binding nature.

85. The Supreme Court of Pakistan expressed a similar view as to the disability of an employee of a Provincial Industrial Development Corporation in seeking redress against his dismissal from the service of the said Corporation in the case of The Chairman, East Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation and another Vs. Rustom Ali and another, 19 D.L.R. (SC) 186 same case P.L.D. 1966 S.C. 848 on which strong reliance has been placed on behalf of the appellants. The Dacca High Court gave declaration on a petition filed by Rustom Ali, the dismissed employee, under Article 98 of the Pakistan Constitution that the order of dismissal was without lawful authority and of no legal effect, as the Secretary of the Corporation who passed the order of dismissal was not competent to dismiss him. The Supreme Court, on appeal, being of the view that the case was governed by the law declared in The Lahore Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. Vs. Pir Saifullah Khan 12 D.L.R. (S.C.) 108, held that the service of the respondent was subject to the ordinary rule of master and servant and as such he was not entitled to any such declaration. From a question of a certain passage from the earlier judgment in the case of The Lahore Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. in which it was recited that the Superior of Court in England issued writ of mandamus for restoration to office of public nature only and did not extend its scope to private corporation, it appears that the learned Judges were of the opinion that the Court could make an appropriate order for restoration to an office having a public character, but that Industrial Development Corporation of East Pakistan having had no public character and having been rarely a private Corporation, no remedy could be granted in writ jurisdiction.

86. It is difficult to concur with the view as expressed in this judgment as to the character of the Corporation concerned, but no exception may perhaps be taken to the proposition of law which appears to have been laid down in the said case, namely, that the Court has power to issue a writ requiring restoration of a dismissed employee to an office of public nature. What office can be said to be of public nature does not appear to have been analysed and examined in any of the decisions of the Pakistan Supreme Court. In three of the earlier cases viz. The Lahore Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. Vs. Pir Saifullah Khan, Faiz Ahmed Vs. Registrar, Co-operative Societies Ltd. and Zainul Abedin Vs. Mutton CO-operative Bank Ltd, the Corporation concerned were co-operative Banks which, though subject to some kind of control of the Provincial Government through the Registrar Co-operative Societies, were not considered to have sufficient public character, whereas the Corporation concerned in the case of The Managing Committee of Co-operative Model Town Society Ltd. Vs. Khan Mohammad lqbal, though a co-operative society was considered to have some kind of public character.

87. If we examine the object, structure and mode of operation of East Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation, there is hardly any scope for doubt that it was a public corporation. It was set up under the Central Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1962 under the exclusive control of the Government for the purpose of promoting economic and industrial development of East Pakistan which was undoubtedly a public purpose. The general direction and administration of the Corporation and its affairs vested in a Board of Directors, all of whom were to be appointed by the Government and who were guided by such directions, as the Government might give it from time to time. The learned Judges deciding Rustom Ali's case themselves found that East Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation was a person within the meaning of Article 98(2) of the then Pakistan Constitution and such a finding at once established the public character of the Corporation, as such a Corporation could not be a person within the meaning of the said constitutional provision unless it performed functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority. As the specific character of the said Corporation was not closely examined and its distinguishing features from those of the institutions which are considered private, were noticed in Rustom Ali's case, the said decision is not at all helpful for the correct under-standing of the law on the subject.

<u>88. The Supreme Court of Pakistan held in the case of Eastern Mercantile Bank Ltd. Vs. Mohammad Shamsuddin 21 D.L.R. (S.C.) 368 which arose out of a suit that the service of the appellant, who was a local Manager on probation was no more than of contractual nature and that as such the termination of the service before the: expiry of the probationary period did not entitle the appellant to sue for a declaration as to the invalidity of the said order. It was a case of a private Corporation and there was no case of violation of any statutory provision, and as such no objection can be raised to the said decision.</u>

<u>89. The case of Secretary EPIDC Vs. Serajul Huq 22 D.L.R. (S.C.) 284, however, stands on a different footing, as the EPIDC, as we have already seen, was a public Corporation. But it was found by the Supreme Court of Pakistan that the terms and conditions of employment of the respondents were not regulated by any statutory rules, but were governed by their contracts of employment, and on the said premise it was held that the ordinary rule of master and servant was applicable to that case. It was also pointed out that the termination in question having not been effected by way of penalty, the question of affording opportunity of showing cause against the said order of termination did not arise. This case unmistakably expresses the view that in case of termination of service of an employee of the Corporation on certain charges, the employee concerned was entitled to challenge the validity of the said order on the ground of the violation of the principle of natural justice.</u>

90. Learned Attorney-General has also cited an unreported decision of the High Court Division of this Court in the case of Dr. Md. Abdul Muttalib Vs. University of Dacca and others, to which one of us was a party, where the validity of the order of discharge of the petitioner, who was the Medical Officer on probation, was challenged but it has been held in the said case that the petitioner being a probationer, his service was not controlled by any statutory rule or regulation. It has been noticed in the judgment that there was no case of violation of any regulation made out in the petition but that it was sought to be so argued at the time of the hearing, and although in repelling the said argument it has been observed relying upon the two Indian Supreme Court decisions in the cases of The U.P. Warehousing Corporation Vs. Chandra Kiron, and Indian Air Lines Corporation Vs. Sukhdeo, but without critically examining the rationale of the said two cases, that the Regulations relating to the terms and conditions of service made by the University under statutory powers have no statutory force, but it has been as a matter of, found that there was no such violation of any statutory provision.

91. A review of all these decisions, as have been referred to above shows that preponderance of judicial authorities have helped the formulation of certain well-reasoned principles as to the law relating to the employees of a statutory corporation as administered by the Superior Courts in their writ jurisdiction as well as by the ordinary civil Courts. We are concerned in these two appeals with the statutory bodies of public character, viz. Bangladesh Small Industries Corporation and Janata Bank, and the law governing the employees of such bodies may be briefly stated as follows:-

(a) If an employee is dismissed or his service is terminated in contravention of a mandatory statutory provision, the employee has a right of action either in a Superior Court in its writ jurisdiction or in a Civil Court.

(b) If the service of its employee is terminated in violation of the principle of natural justice, the employee has a similar right of action as in (a).

(c) If the office is a statutory one, the holder of the office has similar right of action as in (a) in case of termination of the said office not in accordance with the law, under which the said office has been created. (d) In spite of the office being a statutory one or of public character, terms and conditions of the office may be regulated by contract, and termination of service in contravention of such contract, but otherwise than in the manner mentioned in (a) and (b) is not actionable for the purpose of reinstatement in the office. (e) Terms and conditions of service prescribed by rules, regulations or any other form of delegated legislation made by a body under statutory powers are not contractual, but have statutory force and the dismissal or termination of service in substantial disregard of them will entitle the employee to a right of action as in(a).

92. We have already noticed that an employee of a statutory Corporation cannot claim the status of one in the service of the Republic, but the public character of such an employee has been recognised in a number of legislative enactments where such an employee has been given—although for the purposes of the said enactments—the status of a 'Government Servant' or a 'Public Servant'. A detailed examination of these legislative measures is not necessary except for the purpose of examining their bearing on the character of the Corporation. It appears that President's Order No. 25 of 1973 provides for recruitment of certain categories of officers of statutory corporations on the recommendations of the Public Service Commission set up under the Constitution. Furthermore, the General Clauses Act has now been amended and by an inclusive definition, all statutory corporations are now Local Authorities. Such a definition unmistakably underlines the public character of these Corporations.

93. To approach the question whether a dismissed employee of a statutory corporation is entitled to declaration of nullity from a court, it is first to be seen what is the character of the corporation, secondly, what is the statutory provision with regard to the post the i employee is holding, whether its created by the statute or created under the statutory power. The holder of the former is a person holding a statutory post, but not the latter. Thirdly, whether any statutory status has been conferred on the employee though the post held by him is created under a statutory power. Fourthly, whether there is any statutory restriction on the Corporation as to the kind of contract it can make or the grounds on which it can dismiss. Where therefore the post of an employee of a statutory corporation has some public character or he holds or enjoys a statutory post or status, he cannot be dismissed without a precedent hearing, no matter whether there is any other statutory rule or regulation in that behalf. Precedent hearing or compliance of the principles of the natural justice is implicit in the dismissal of employee enjoying some statutory status or holding a statutory post or a post of a public character. If there be any justice rule framed by the Corporation under statutory powers substantial compliance of justice rule is mandatory because that will supply the natural justice rule and dismissal of such an employee without precedent hearing will entitle him to get declaration of nullity from a Court of law.

94. Again an employee of a statutory Corporation of public character, who does not hold any statutory post or status can nevertheless maintain an action in a Court of law, on a limited ground, that of violation of any mandatory statutory provision as to the kind of contract or the statutory ground of dismissal, or on the doctrine of ultra vires or the violation of the rule of natural justice.

<u>95. We now turn to the merits of the appeal. The learned Attorney-General strenuously urged that the principle governing the relationship between Master and Servant would apply in the facts and accordingly he took us to the provisions of Bangladesh Small and Cottage Industries Corporation Act, 1957 (Act XVII of 1957), hereinafter referred to as the Act. Under Section 3(2) of the Act the appellant is a body corporate by the name of Small and Cottage Industries Corporation, subject to the provisions of the Act, to acquire and hold property, both moveable, and immoveable and shall by the said name sue and be sued. Under Section 4(3) of the Act the Bangladesh Government shall be a share-holder of the Corporation and shall subscribe to and hold not less than fifty-one per cent of the shares issued by the Corporation at any time; the remaining shares shall be reserved for public subscriptions. The management of the Corporation has been vested in a Board of Directors under Sections 6 and 7 of the Act consisting not more than five and all appointed by the Government. Under section 9(1) of the Act Bangladesh Government is required to appoint one of the Director of the Board who shall be the Chief Executive of the Corporation. Under section 13 of the Act, the Corporation may appoint or employ such persons as it considers necessary for the efficient performance of its functions. Section 45 of the Act provides for making rules by the Government not inconsistent with this Act for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of this Act and where the regulations framed under section 46 of the Act are inconsistent with the rules, the rules shall prevail. Under section 46(1) of the Act the Board may, with the previous sanction of the Government, make regulations not inconsistent with this Act or the rules made under this Act to provide for all matters for which provisions is necessary or expedient for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of this Act. Under section 46(2) (h) of the Act the Board has been empowered to make regulations for the terms and conditions of service, duties and conduct of officers, servants and agents of the Corporation. The regulations have been framed under section 46(2)(k) and the regulations so framed were published in the Extraordinary Dacca Gazette on 3rd May, 1965.</u>

<u>98. Bearing the principles adumbrated above, we find that majority of the shares is held by the Government but public subscription is also considerable. However, the management and control of the Corporation is vested in a Board of Directors, not exceeding five and all appointed by the Government. Though there is public subscription of shares, there is no public participation in the management and control of the Corporation. If we turn to the function and object of the Corporation, we observe that principal aim is to help promote small industries by giving loan, advice and sometime starting project and then selling it to prospective investors. The purpose is public service, it is promotional and for development for the benefit and service of the community, and not for any profitable commercial undertaking. The Corporation has a definite public service in view viz., to promote small industries and help their investors. It has therefore a public character. Its employees partake of that public Character.</u>

<u>99. Along with it is to be noted that by the provision of General Clauses Act, this statutory Corporation is deemed to be a local authority. Local authority connotes a kind of public administration. Again by various legislative measures set out above the employee of statutory corporations have sometimes been described as Government servants and some-times as public servants. No doubt each of this legislative enactments is limited to the purpose of its own, nonetheless it cannot be denied that the cumulative effect of these legislative measures have at least clothed them with some public character.</u>

<u>100. The Act itself has provided that for criminal misconduct the employees of this Corporation shall be deemed to be public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Penal Code. It would be unjust to hold that an employee of this Corporation will be punished for misconduct as a Public Servant but dismissed like private servant. The public character of his employment give him at least the benefit of precedent hearing. He is entitled to a hearing before his dismissal, whether there is and not justice rule provided in the statutory rule. He can maintain an action for a declaration of nullity.</u>

<u>From the above discussion, it appears that the respondent cannot be treated on the general principle of Master and Servant. We are therefore not called upon to consider the further question whether the High Court Division was justified in holding that charges levelled against the respondent did not amount to misconduct warranting dismissal and whether they were proved against him. The question is outside the scope of the leave order and so we abstain from entering into it.</u>

In the result this appeal is dismissed with no order as to cost.
